Vocabulary
running / discoveryrunning your app is executing — a step running, or the SDK reporting what runs next
okgood step.run() returned
failedbad step.run() threw
stoppedstopped executing when the run was cancelled
childchild step.invoke() child run
waitingwait step.sleep(), step.waitForEvent() or step.waitForSignal(), not resolved
sleep / matchedwaitok step.sleep() elapsed, or a wait matched
timed outwaitout the wait expired with no match
backoffbackoff retry backoff before the next attempt
span okspanok a userland span that reported OK
span errorspanerr a userland span that reported ERROR
spanspanunset a userland span that set no status — the common case
heldhold held by concurrency, throttle, rate limit or debounce
queuedidle waiting for the executor to pick it up
queuedqueued enqueued, not started
plannedribbon enqueued by a discovery request that reported several steps
startedhollow execution started
retryhollow-bad the attempt threw, another will follow
donedone resolved, and no status was reported — OpenTelemetry Unset
okok resolved, succeeded
failedfailed threw on the final attempt
timeouttimeout the wait expired with no match
cancelledcancelled the run was cancelled

Hollow and filled is a rule, not a preference. It reports whether the row has resolved, so it is not adjustable.

Trace Design System

How Inngest draws a function run. The vocabulary is in the panel on the left and is live: change it there and every figure on this page changes.

Moments

Inngest records a run as spans. A span carries timestamps: when the step was enqueued, when the SDK started executing it, when it resolved. Those timestamps are what the trace has.

Durations

The interval between two timestamps is what you want to read.

A step’s lifecycle

Every step reaches the same states whatever its type: enqueued, executing, resolved. A step that throws adds an attempt and a backoff and goes round again.

Two rules

Marks report whether something has resolved.

  • hollow: not resolved
  • filled: resolved. Only a resolution is green or red.

Bars report whether the SDK was executing.

  • solid: your function was running
  • hatched: it was not
Colour says what kind. Fill says whether the SDK was executing, for a bar, and whether it has resolved, for a mark. The full set is in the panel on the left.

Structure

A discovery request is the SDK reporting what to run next. When one reports more than one step, it gets its own bar and a ribbon down to the steps it reported.

A discovery bar appears only where the request reported more than one step. A request that reported one step, which is the next step in a chain or the step after a coalesce, is a single execution and rolls into that step’s row.

The Run row

Today the Run row is a full width bar in the run’s status colour. The header, the status badge and the axis already report that. It could instead report where the elapsed time went.

Compressed time

A run can be nine days elapsed and five seconds executing. Dead time is worth almost none of the width, and the threshold is low: anything with nothing executing for more than a few percent of the run collapses to a band, and an hour and a week get the same few pixels.

Only the drawing compresses. Every reported duration is still wall clock.

The width left over is split between the surviving stretches in proportion to their real duration, which is the same thing as saying a second is worth the same number of pixels wherever it lands. Two spans either side of a compressed gap stay comparable, and several compressions need no special case.

The bands share one budget, so a run full of idle stretches does not spend its width on the parts where nothing happened. They thin instead, and below a width that can hold them a band drops its label, then its tear, leaving a marked line. The rules and the blur never go — they are what says not to scale.

Your server, in detail

A step instrumented with @inngest/otel reports what your code did inside it — HTTP calls, database queries, third-party APIs. Everything above this point is Inngest’s own timing; this is the first thing in the trace that is not.

They are your code at finer grain, so they keep the status colours a step has. What separates them from a step is nesting and weight, not a new colour: a span is a subdivision of the bar above it, never a peer of it.

The same at any complexity. Spans inside a Promise.all overlap, and on their own pitch that reads as exactly what it is — several things running at once inside one step — without a ribbon, a mark or an ordering claim, none of which apply to something the trace did not schedule.

A span is a plain bar on a tighter pitch: no queue mark, no start, no resolution circle. The event vocabulary belongs to the trace, and a span is something that happened inside one row of it.

The nesting is a claim, and the trace has to be able to keep it.

The selected row

A row is plotted against the whole run, so a step that took ten seconds inside a twenty minute run is a few pixels wide and its marks overlap. Selecting it replots that row across the full width using the same bars and marks, and names each piece: intervals with their durations, marks with what happened. Hover a piece for its description.

This is not a second way of drawing a run. Same bars, same marks, more width.

Annotations

Optional, usually a duration. The annotation sits after the row’s last bar rather than in a fixed column, so it takes no horizontal space and disappears when there is nothing to report.

Scenarios

Organised by what you wrote. One code example, then everything the trace shows for it — ordered from a single step to the cases that are hard to draw. Where a figure has a second state, it is the hover or selection.

await step.run('a', …)
  • The step returned: solid green bar, filled green resolution mark. The baseline everything else reads against.
  • The hatched stretch in front of it is queue time — the step enqueued, waiting for the executor to pick it up.
  • System latency is the same substance and is named the same way. Three greys for three kinds of waiting would be three things to learn for no gain.
  • Everything Inngest did is hatched and only SDK execution is solid, so the eye lands on your code first.

Held by flow control. Amber hatched — queue time with a reason, still not SDK execution time.

Finalization keeps its own row and is not SDK execution time.

Every millisecond between a row’s start and its resolution belongs to a named interval — here the queue, a failed attempt, its backoff, the queue again, and the attempt that worked.

  • A row’s label and its drawing have to agree about which interval the number names.
  • Nothing is drawn that cannot be asked what it is: every interval and every mark decomposes into named parts on hover.
await step.run('a', …)
await step.run('b', …)

One request, one step. The SDK reports and executes in the same request, so there is no discovery bar.

A discovery request is a separate execution. It happens at the start of a run and on fan-out.

The gap between a step resolving and the next request starting is drawn once, as the cable and as the interval.

await Promise.all([
  step.run('a', …),
  step.run('b', …),
  step.run('c', …),
])

// a step outside the fan-out
await step.run('unrelated', …)

One request reports three steps. The ribbon threads their enqueue marks, which are blue because a discovery request put them there.

The ribbon covers exactly the steps the request reported, so an uneven fan-out is countable without interacting. Nothing static predicted that width.

Throttle, rate limit and debounce are the same fact and take the same treatment.

await Promise.all([
  step.run('a', …),
  step.run('b', …),
  step.run('c', …),
])
await step.run('d', …)

Three steps resolve and cause the next request. That request reported one step, so it rolls into that step’s row.

Three tiers of attention: the row, what caused it, everything else. Nothing is removed, only quietened.

The Run row is the overview. One picture of the run, not two.

Where the trace cannot say what caused a request, it declines rather than guessing.

await step.run('a', …)

await Promise.all([
  step.run('b', …),
  step.run('c', …),
])

One resumption reports two steps. Both sit under one ribbon, so no order is implied between them.

await Promise.all([
  step.run('a', …),
  step.run('b', …),
])
await Promise.all([
  step.run('a1', …),
  step.run('a2', …),
])
await step.run('b1', …)

Fan-out inside a fan-out. One ribbon per discovery request.

await Promise.all([
  (async () => {
    await step.run('a', …)
    await step.run('a2', …)
  })(),
  (async () => {
    await step.run('b', …)
    await step.run('b2', …)
  })(),
])

Two branches that each caused their own request. Two requests, no ribbon.

await Promise.race([
  step.run('fast', …),
  step.run('slow', …),
])
await step.run('next', …)

The winner is a dependency of the next request. The loser resolved after that request started, so it has no cable.

await step.run('a', …)

// started, never awaited
step.run('orphan', …)

await step.run('b', …)

A step started but never awaited. No outgoing cable.

const ids =
  await step.sendEvent('notify', [
    { name: 'app/thing' },
  ])

step.sendEvent() is the one row that points out of the run. The ring is hollow because those runs are not in this trace, and the count is the way into them.

await step.run('doomed', async () => {
  throw new Error('boom')
})

It threw on the final attempt and the run failed.

Every attempt threw. The only place a circle is filled red.

await step.run('flaky', async () => {
  if (attempt < 2)
    throw new Error('flaky')
  return 'ok'
})

Threw, backed off, retried, returned. The backoff is the consequence of the failure, not a failure itself.

try {
  await step.run('caught', async () => {
    throw new Error('boom')
  })
} catch {}

await step.run('after', …)

The function caught the error. Red step, green run.

await Promise.all([
  step.run('ok-branch', …),
  step.run('bad-branch', …),
])
await step.run('after', …)

One red row does not tint the rows around it.

await step.run('landed', …)
await step.run('still going', …)

Still executing. Blue, and no resolution mark: the missing mark is what says it is unresolved.

await Promise.all([
  step.run('a', …),
  step.run('b', …),   // still running
])
// the run was cancelled

Cancelled while executing.

await step.waitForEvent('waiting', {
  event: 'x',
  timeout: '1h',
})
// still open when the run
// was cancelled

A wait still open when the run was cancelled.

await step.run('a', …)

await step.waitForEvent('w', {
  event: 'app/paid',
  timeout: '1h',
})

// on match
await step.run('b', …)
// on timeout
await step.run('fallback', …)

A wait that matched. Blue while it is open, green at the mark where the event arrived.

A wait that expired with no match. The run carries on: a timeout is a result the function can act on.

await Promise.all([
  step.run('a', …),
  step.run('b', …),
  step.waitForEvent('c', {
    event: 'x',
    timeout: '1h',
  }),
])
await step.run('d', …)

A wait inside a fan-out holds the level open. The next request cannot start until the slowest member resolves.

await step.sleep('nap', '2s')

await step.run('a', async () => {
  throw new Error('boom')
})

Waiting and failing must not read alike. One is hatched and never red; the other is solid and red.

await step.run('a', …)
await step.sleep('nap', '7d')
await step.run('b', …)

Dead time is worth almost none of the width. The threshold is low, the band is fixed, and only the drawing compresses — every duration is still wall clock.

Seven days elapsed, 62ms executing. The fill rule reports that before you have read a number.

A step too short to draw is still drawn, at a minimum width, with its real duration beside it.

A wait that has not resolved still compresses. No closing mark, and no Finalization row: the run is still going.

await step.run('left', …)     // 30s
await step.sleep('gap', '7d')
await step.run('right', …)    // 10s

The width left over splits by real duration, so a second is the same number of pixels wherever it lands.

for (const i of items) {          // 9
  await step.run('poll', …)
  await step.sleep('nap', '2m')
}

Many compressions share one budget. Each band thins rather than the trace spending its width on nothing.

await Promise.all([
  (async () => {
    await step.run('a', …)
    await step.sleep('a', '18s')
  })(),
  step.run('b', …),
])
await step.sleep('c', '15m')
await step.run('c', …)
await step.run('d', …)

A gap in one row is not dead time. Only a stretch with nothing running anywhere is a candidate.

// a run measured in days
// keeps its resolution

Two tiers of axis label, so a run measured in days keeps its resolution without a second axis.

await step.run('setup', …)

for (const i of items) {        // 500
  await step.run('fetch', …)
}

await step.run('teardown', …)

Five hundred sequential steps collapse to one row that reports the count and draws where each member ran.

await Promise.all(
  items.map(() =>                // 12
    step.run('worker', …)),

await step.run('collect', …)

A wide fan-out collapses the same way. The stagger of a concurrency limit is visible without expanding it.

for (const i of items) {
  // a cluster of these threw
  await step.run('act', …)
}

A failure cluster two thirds through a long run is a red smear on the Run row, findable without interacting.

await step.run('first', …)

for (const i of items) {        // 40
  await step.run('batch', …)
}

await step.run('last', …)

About forty rows at rest whatever the step count, and any group expands where you are standing.

await Promise.all([
  step.run('fetch', …),
  step.run('fetch', …),
])
// coalescing after the Promise.all
// reports one step, so it rolls
// into that step's row
await step.run('save', …)

The same step name on two branches. The name is not the identity; the request that reported it is.

The SDK’s :1 and :2 suffixes are not stable under parallelism, so nothing in the drawing depends on them.

await step.run('a', …)
// the request reporting b

A step instrumented with @inngest/otel. The icon by the name says there are spans inside; selecting the row expands them.

Expanded. Everything above this point is Inngest’s own timing; these rows are the first thing in the trace that is not.

  await Promise.all([

User docs

The page we would ship, rendered from docs/understanding-traces.md with its figures resolved to the live drawings. If a rule changes and this stops being true, that is the signal.

Every function run produces a trace: one row per thing that happened, on one time axis. It shows what your code did, what Inngest did around it, and where the time actually went.

Two rules cover almost all of it.

The two rules

Bars are intervals. Colour says what kind of work, fill says whether your code was running.

SolidYour function was executing. This is the part you pay for.
HatchedNothing of yours was running — queued, sleeping, waiting, backing off.

Circles are moments. Hollow means unresolved, filled means resolved.

Only a resolution circle is ever green or red. Everything before it is neutral, so the outcome of a row is always the last thing on it.

That is the whole encoding. Two sequential steps, read left to right:

Reading a row

A step's row runs left to right through its own life:

  1. queued — grey hollow circle. Enqueued, waiting for a worker.
  2. A hatched bar — the wait. Costs nothing.
  3. started — white hollow circle. Your code began.
  4. A solid bar — your code running.
  5. ok, failed or timeout — filled. The row resolved.

A row with no final circle has not resolved. That missing circle is the signal — a step still running is drawn blue with nothing closing it.

Requests, and why some rows start blue

Inngest does not know your whole function up front. It calls your app, your code runs until it hits something it has to hand back, and the SDK reports what comes next. That call is a discovery request, and it is drawn in blue.

A discovery request is a request like any other, so it has the same lifecycle: queued, then a wait, then it starts, then it runs.

What happens at the end of it is the interesting part.

Sequential code — the request finds one step and runs it. No handoff, no second call. The blue turns green when the step returns, and the row ends on one ok.

await step.run('a', …)
await step.run('b', …)

Parallel code — the request finds several steps. It cannot run them all here, so it reports them and stops. The next circle is planned, the only blue hollow circle in the trace, and a ribbon drops from it to every step that request reported.

await Promise.all([
  step.run('a', …),
  step.run('b', …),
  step.run('c', …),
])

Each of those steps then starts its own cycle: queued, wait, started, run.

The ribbon

The ribbon is the vertical line threading the planned circles of steps that came from one request. It is drawn at rest, not on hover, so:

  • Count the ribbon to see how wide a fan-out was, without clicking anything.
  • Steps under one ribbon have no order between them. They were reported together.
  • Two ribbons means two requests. Two branches that each scheduled their own work do not share one.

When those steps all resolve, they cause the next request:

An uneven fan-out is countable at rest — you can see it produced three without counting them:

Ribbons nest, so depth reads without indentation.

Waiting

step.sleep() and step.waitForEvent() are hatched, always. Your code is not running and you are not billed for the wait.

Blue hatchedStill open. Undecided.
Green circleThe sleep elapsed, or the event arrived.
Grey circleThe wait expired with no match.

A timeout is not a failure. It is a result your function can act on, so the row goes grey and the run carries on.

Failure and recovery

  • One red step in a green run means your code caught the error. The step failed; the run did not.
  • A retry shows every attempt on one row — a red attempt, the backoff, then a green one. The backoff is hatched, because nothing of yours is running and you are not billed for it, and faded red, because it is a consequence of the failure rather than a failure itself. The attempts carry the alarm.
  • A filled red circle appears only when every attempt failed.
  • Failure never spreads. A red row does not tint its neighbours.

A caught error is a red step inside a green run:

Cancelled is its own state. A step running when a run was cancelled is neither success nor failure, so it ends in a square rather than a circle.

Long runs

A run can be nine days elapsed and five seconds executing, so idle stretches are worth almost none of the width. Anything longer than a few percent of the run collapses to a narrow band — an hour and a week get the same few pixels, because the space belongs to the work.

The band is marked three ways: the Run row's own track tears, rules cross every row at both edges, and whatever runs through the band is blurred.

Everything left over shares one scale. The width freed up is split between the surviving stretches in proportion to how long they really took — 30 seconds of work on one side of a gap and 10 on the other get 75% and 25% of it. So a second is the same width wherever it lands, and two steps either side of a compressed gap are still worth comparing.

A run with many idle stretches does not fill up with bands: they share a fixed budget and get thinner, down to a single marked line.

Only the axis compresses. Every duration stays wall clock. A step that took 890ms says 890ms whatever the axis is doing.

Reading the fill alone tells you the compute-to-elapsed ratio before you read a number — here, seven days elapsed and 62ms executing:

A step too short to draw still gets drawn, at a minimum width, with its real duration beside it. The drawing rounds; the number does not.

Big runs

At a few hundred steps, a full list stops being readable. Repeated steps that share a shape collapse into one row that reports the count and draws where each member ran.

A collapsed group tells you what varied:

38 × search, 2 × write_file

That is usually what you opened the trace to find. Iteration 7 calling a different tool is the interesting one, and collapsing by shape is what surfaces it. Expand any group in place.

The Run row

The top row is the whole run: a grey track of elapsed time, coloured wherever your code was executing. It is the overview — one picture of the run, at the same scale as everything under it.

Any failure in a stretch colours it red. So a cluster of failures two thirds through a 500-step run is a red smear on that one row, visible before you scroll or click anything.

Click a cluster to jump to it.

What the trace will not tell you

Worth knowing, so you do not go looking:

  • Why a branch was not taken. A run records what happened, not what didn't.
  • What caused a request, when nothing reported it. Where the trace cannot say, it declines rather than guessing — you will see a note, not a line.
  • Anything outside a step. A bare inngest.send() outside step.sendEvent() has no span, so nothing ties it to what it triggered.

Where the view is inferring rather than reading a reported fact, it says so rather than letting a guess look like something that was reported.

Scrub a real run

Each fixture is a captured run at its measured proportions, shown complete. Drag the slider to move back through every intermediate state: rows appear as their spans are created, intervals that have not finished are blue because their outcome is not decided yet, and the axis rescales so the elapsed part always fills the width.

step Three steps around a step.sleep(). Each step resolving causes a request to your app to report what runs next; that request is the short blue interval at the head of the next row. At real proportions it is 1ms against a 2s sleep, so it is only visible while the axis is still short.

v4sequential A chain on an SDK that can report batches. Every request reported exactly one step, so no request gets a row of its own and there is no ribbon anywhere. Each one is the blue interval at the head of the step it reported.

100%complete

invoke step.invoke(). The row opens with queue time, then the blue request that reported the step, then the child run in its own colour on this run’s axis. The child is 61% of the parent and the parent does nothing while it runs.

Connect

Connect changes the transport, not the spans. Same span names, same shape, same step ops, so nothing above needs a Connect variant.

Two differences sit inside the spans. A Connect run carries no inngest.http.timing, so there is no network breakdown to expand. The connect proxy polls for the SDK response every 2s plus a random 0 to 3s; when its push is missed that wait lands inside the execution span with nothing marking it, so the execution figure over reports.
